A. INTRODUCTION
While Congress and the president often concern themselves with high- 
profile issues affecting the federal government’s structure and policy 
priorities, inside the typical government agency much of the work involves 
gathering information and using it to make decisions about particular 
individuals, organizations, or situations. In American public law, we use 
the term “adjudication” to describe this eclectic mix of agency action that— 
instead of involving a prospective agency policy or rule—^resolves a discrete 
dispute or Hotormines the legal consequences of circumstances affecting 
particular parties.
Although the very term “administrative adjudication” threatens to 
dampen interest, a quick tour of examples is sufficient to demonstrate the 
critical importance of this vast domain of agency action. Adjudication may 
be used to make high-profile, politically charged decisions, such as:
• 
The Atomic Energy Commission’s 1954 decision to revoke Dr. 
Robert Oppenheimer’s security clearance;
• 
The Food and Drug Administration’s 2011 decision 
concerning the safety and efficacy of so-called “Plan B” 
contraceptive drugs; and
• 
The Federal Aviation Administration’s grounding of the 
Boeing 737 Max following two crashes of the popular aircraft.
In other cases, adjudication may involve decisions that, although 
individually less salient, are essential to protecting the public interest, 
such as when:
An Occupational Safety and Health Administration inspector 
determines that a fire extinguisher is improperly located in a 
workshop;
The Federal Trade Commission determines that a proposed 
merger is anticompetitive; or
A Consumer Product Safety Commission investigator 
determines that a product does not conform to design or 
manufacturing standards.
